title: Merit not held (section 28)
hookLine: the bodhisattva does not take hold of merit

lines: WHERE DOES A GOOD DEED GO?
cards: Where does a good deed go once it's done? Some of us file it. A volunteer shift in one drawer, a favor for a friend in another, and on a bad night we open the cabinet and count.
Proof that we're decent. Buddhists have a word for the good that flows from good actions; in English it's usually called merit. Section twenty-eight of the Diamond Sutra doesn't say merit is fake.
It says something stranger about what a bodhisattva does with it.

teach.b: It starts with a comparison the sutra has used before, with a new winner. One bodhisattva fills worlds as many as the sands of the Ganges with jewels and gives them all away.
Another comes to a patient acceptance that all things are without a self and unborn. The second, the Buddha says, makes the greater merit. A heap of jewels loses to a quiet change of mind.
And yet a bodhisattva does not take hold of merit. The good is made. It isn't grabbed.
Subhuti asks a fair question, in paraphrase: shouldn't a bodhisattva gain merit? The answer threads a needle. Gain it, yes.
It is gained, and that's exactly why it isn't to be held, and why it's only called merit gained. Merit is real enough to make, and too alive to keep in a drawer.
Back on day one hundred forty-three you met the dedication of merit, and in some Buddhist communities a sitting or a chant still ends that way: whatever good came from this, may it go out to others.
The merit is made, then handed on before anyone can count it.
It's like a river running through a farm.
The water is real, the crops drink it, and nobody owns the river. A filing cabinet fills up and waits to be opened. A river fills the field and keeps moving.

how: In some Theravada and Mahayana communities, a sitting, chant or offering can end by dedicating its merit to others, so the good that was made is shared rather than kept.

o: merit belongs only to monks, never to lay people
good deeds earn nothing, so there's no point in them
a bodhisattva makes merit but doesn't take hold of it

s: the sutra says merit isn't real
it's made and gained; what the bodhisattva doesn't do is take hold of it.
Subhuti asks whether a bodhisattva should gain merit
and the Buddha answers: gain it, but don't take hold of it.
in section 28 the heap of jewels wins
patient acceptance that all things are selfless and unborn makes the greater merit.

games.q: you've been told a bodhisattva doesn't take hold of merit. you're Subhuti. what do you ask?
o: then why do good at all?
games.why: Subhuti asks it, and the Buddha threads the needle: gain it, yes; take hold of it, no. so it's called merit gained.

practice: Think of one good thing you've done lately, small is fine: a meal cooked, a patient answer, an hour given. See it plainly, notice any wish to file it away as proof, and then gently open the hand.
Let the good of it go out past you, to the person it touched and on to anyone who needs it, the way water leaves a field.

wordCard.voice: Merit not held. Section twenty-eight: a bodhisattva makes merit, and gains it, but doesn't take hold of it. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: patience, patient acceptance; in section 28, the acceptance that things are selfless and unborn outweighs worlds of jewels.

carryVoice: Your line: not held. Made, gained, and handed on. Rest well, and I'll see you tomorrow.
